italy.name: Italy
steps: Get a codice fiscale
Your Italian tax code. It is free, from the Agenzia delle Entrate in Italy or an Italian consulate abroad.
Make a written offer
The proposta d'acquisto usually comes with a small deposit. Once accepted, many buyers sign a preliminary contract (compromesso) with a 10–30% deposit.
Check the house
Ask for the land registry extract (visura catastale), proof the building matches its plans (conformità urbanistica e catastale), the energy certificate (APE) and any unpaid debts on the property.
Sign at the notary
The deed (rogito) is signed before a notaio, who checks the title and registers the sale. You can sign by power of attorney if you cannot travel.
Pay the taxes
Buying from a private seller: registration tax 9% of the cadastral value for a second home, or 2% if it becomes your main home, plus €50 + €50 fixed taxes and the notary's fee.
italy.yearly: IMU (council property tax) on second homes and a local waste tax (TARI). For small rural houses these are often a few hundred euros a year.

spain.name: Spain
steps: Get an NIE
Your foreigner identity number, from a Spanish consulate or a police station in Spain. You need it to sign and to pay taxes.
Open a Spanish bank account
Most notaries and councils expect payments and bills to go through a Spanish account.
Reserve with an arras contract
A private contract with a deposit, usually 10%. If the seller backs out, they normally return it twice.
Check the house
Order a nota simple from the Land Registry (owner and debts). In the countryside, check the land status (suelo rústico) and that the buildings are legal. Ask for the last IBI receipts.
Sign at the notary and register
The escritura is signed before a notario and then registered at the Registro de la Propiedad.
Pay the transfer tax
Resale homes pay ITP of 6–10% depending on the region, plus notary and registry of roughly €1,000–2,000.
spain.yearly: IBI (council tax) and waste collection. Non-residents who do not rent the house out also file a small yearly imputed-income tax.

portugal.name: Portugal
steps: Get a NIF
Your tax number, at a Finanças office or through a representative. Non-EU residents usually need a fiscal representative.
Sign a promissory contract
The CPCV fixes price and date, with a deposit of 10–30%.
Check the house
Ask for the caderneta predial and the certidão permanente (owner, debts, urban or rustic), and the habitation licence (licença de utilização).
Sign the deed
At a notary or a Casa Pronta office, then the sale is registered at the Conservatória.
Pay the taxes
IMT on a sliding scale up to about 8% (5% on rustic land) and stamp duty of 0.8%.
portugal.yearly: IMI (council tax), usually 0.3–0.45% of the tax value for urban property.

denmark.name: Denmark
steps: Check if you need permission
Use Civilstyrelsen's rules: EU/EEA citizens living in Denmark sign a declaration, everyone else applies for permission for the specific property.
Get a Danish tax number
If you have no Danish personal number, request one from the Danish Tax Agency with form 04.063_AP_EN.
Set a budget with a bank
Danish banks usually lend up to 80% of the value, so plan for at least a 20% down payment.
Make an offer and sign with conditions
The seller's agent drafts the contract; have your own lawyer review it and add bank and lawyer approval clauses (bank- og advokatforbehold).
Let your lawyer check the documents
Your lawyer reviews the condition report, title and registered charges before the clauses are lifted.
Register the deed
The deed (skøde) is registered digitally with the Land Registration Court and the registration fee is paid, which makes you the legal owner.
denmark.yearly: Expect property value tax and municipal land tax, both charged through the Danish tax system, plus insurance, utilities and upkeep. Owners abroad may need to file a Danish tax return if they rent the home out.

sweden.name: Sweden
steps: Get a coordination number
Book an identity check at a Swedish Tax Agency service centre to get a samordningsnummer, which you need to register as owner.
Open a Swedish bank account
A Swedish account is normally needed to complete the payment.
Find a home and arrange money
Listings are on Hemnet and Booli; foreign buyers may face a larger deposit if a bank lends at all.
Inspect before you commit
Visit the property and consider hiring an inspector before signing.
Sign the purchase contract
You and the seller sign the contract, usually with the seller's agent handling the paperwork.
Apply for title at Lantmäteriet
Apply to Lantmäteriet for lagfart and pay the 1.5% stamp duty to be registered as owner.
sweden.yearly: House owners pay the municipal property fee and must file a Swedish tax return if they owe it or have rental income, even when living abroad. Add insurance, utilities and upkeep.

norway.name: Norway
steps: Find a home and get loan approval
Search listings on Finn.no and get pre-approval if you need a mortgage; expect to put down 15 to 25%.
Bid through the agent
Offers go through the seller's agent and bidding rounds can close within 24 hours, so inspect the home first.
Sign the contract
The agent draws up the purchase contract; have a local lawyer review it.
Pay at settlement
The price is paid through an escrow account at closing, and the deed is signed.
Get a D-number if needed
Send Kartverket's D-number application with the deed and a certified passport copy no more than 3 months old.
Register the deed
The deed (skjøte) is registered with Kartverket and the 2.5% document duty and fee are paid.
norway.yearly: Expect municipal property tax where it applies, municipal fees, insurance and upkeep. Costs such as municipal fees and property tax are deductible against rental income.

germany.name: Germany
steps: Find a home and arrange money
Search the portals or use a local agent and get financing in place before signing.
Get independent advice
The notary is neutral and does not act for you, so consider your own lawyer and a survey.
Sign before a notary
The notary drafts the purchase contract and both sides sign it in front of the notary; you can sign through a certified power of attorney from abroad.
Secure a priority notice
The notary registers a priority notice (Vormerkung) in the land register to protect you against other sales.
Pay the transfer tax and the price
Pay the transfer tax when the tax office sends the bill, and pay the price as the contract sets out, often via the notary.
Get registered as owner
The land registry (Grundbuch) enters you as owner once the transfer tax is paid, which can take 3 to 4 months.
germany.yearly: Expect the municipal property tax, insurance, utilities and upkeep. Rental profit is taxable in Germany, so a non-resident landlord deals with a German tax office.

netherlands.name: Netherlands
steps: Get a BSN
Register in person at one of the 19 RNI municipalities with a valid ID to get a citizen service number (BSN).
Set up payment and money
Open an account that can pay the notary on time and arrange financing.
Make an offer
A verbal or email acceptance does not bind you; only a signed written purchase agreement (koopovereenkomst) does.
Use the 3-day cooling-off period
A private buyer can cancel within three days of receiving the signed agreement without giving a reason.
Pay the deposit
The standard agreement usually asks for 10% of the price, or a bank guarantee, paid to the notary.
Sign the deed and register
A Dutch civil-law notary signs the transfer deed and you become owner when it is registered with the Kadaster.
netherlands.yearly: Expect municipal property tax (OZB), insurance and upkeep, and in a flat the owners' association (VvE) contribution. Non-residents also pay box 3 income tax based on the property's value.

france.name: France
steps: Make an offer
Agree the price with the seller, usually through the agent. Budget for notary fees and other costs first.
Sign the preliminary contract
Sign the compromis de vente with a notary (notaire). Add conditions (clauses suspensives) such as getting a mortgage.
Use the cooling-off period
You have 10 days after receiving the signed compromis to withdraw without penalty. The seller cannot withdraw.
Pay the deposit
After the cooling-off period, pay a deposit, usually 10% of the price. You may lose it if you pull out without a valid condition.
Let the notary run checks
The notary checks ownership, boundaries and rights of way and collects the compulsory diagnostic surveys (termites, lead, asbestos).
Sign the final deed
Send the balance and fees to the notary's account before the date, then sign the acte de vente in person or by power of attorney. The notary registers the sale.
france.yearly: Expect the annual taxe foncière, plus taxe d'habitation if the home is a furnished second home, and income tax and social charges on any rent.

poland.name: Poland
steps: Get a PESEL number
Apply for a Polish identification number (PESEL) in Poland, in person or through a lawyer with power of attorney. It is free and usually takes up to seven business days.
Check if you need a permit
Non-EEA buyers of a house or land should apply for an MSWiA permit before buying. Apartments do not need one.
Sign a preliminary agreement
Agree the price and pay a deposit, usually 10%. If you withdraw without cause the seller keeps it; if the seller withdraws they repay double.
Do due diligence
A bilingual lawyer can check the land register (księga wieczysta) for liens, debts, unpaid fees and zoning issues.
Sign the notarial deed
Sign the final deed (akt notarialny) before a notary and pay the fees. The notary files the change with the land register.
Pay the PCC tax
Pay the 2% PCC within 14 days of the deed if the notary has not collected it.
poland.yearly: Yearly costs are the local property tax, which is low for flats, plus income tax on any rent.

greece.name: Greece
steps: Get a Greek tax number
Apply for a tax number (AFM) with your passport. It is free and needed to sign contracts and pay taxes.
Hire a lawyer
A lawyer is not mandatory but is strongly recommended. They can act for you under a power of attorney.
Check the title
The lawyer checks ownership and searches the land registry for mortgages, liens and claims. Non-EU buyers in border areas apply for the permit at this stage.
Sign a private agreement
Sign a preliminary purchase agreement and pay a deposit, usually 5-10%, which you normally lose if you withdraw.
Pay the transfer tax
The notary prepares the transfer tax declaration and you pay the tax before the final deed.
Sign the deed and register it
Sign the final contract before a notary and pay the balance, usually on the same day. The deed is then registered at the local land registry or cadastre.
greece.yearly: Yearly costs are ENFIA and income tax on any rent.

switzerland.name: Switzerland
steps: Check your Lex Koller status
Find out whether you can buy freely or need a permit. People living abroad must get authorisation from the canton before buying.
Arrange financing
Banks usually require at least 20% of the price as equity and test affordability at an interest rate of about 5%.
Find a property and make an offer
Search the main portals and make your offer, usually through the seller's agent.
Sign the deed at a notary
The notary drafts the purchase contract (Kaufvertrag, acte de vente), reads it aloud and both parties sign it.
Register the transfer
The notary files the sale with the land register (Grundbuch, registre foncier). Ownership passes once it is registered, which can take several weeks.
switzerland.yearly: Yearly costs are wealth tax, cantonal property tax where it exists, and tax on imputed rental value (Eigenmietwert) if you use the home yourself. Imputed rental value is due to end on 1 January 2029, and cantons may then add a new tax on second homes.

cyprus.name: Cyprus
steps: Hire a lawyer
Use a Cyprus lawyer to negotiate and draft the sale contract and run the checks.
Check the title
The lawyer searches the District Land Registry for ownership, mortgages, court claims and restrictions, and checks permits and VAT status.
Sign the contract
Sign the sale agreement with the price and payment terms. It is legally binding once signed.
Lodge the contract
Deposit the signed contract at the Land Registry under the Specific Performance Law to protect your right to the title.
Apply for permission if non-EU
Non-EU buyers apply to the Council of Ministers through the District Officer, usually after signing. The title cannot be registered without it.
Transfer the title
Pay the balance and transfer fees, then transfer the title deed at the District Land Registry.
cyprus.yearly: Yearly costs are municipal, sewerage and local authority fees, plus income tax and GHS on any rent.

united-kingdom.name: United Kingdom
steps: Make an offer
Make an offer through the seller's estate agent. Acceptance is not binding until contracts are exchanged.
Instruct a solicitor
Hire a solicitor or licensed conveyancer. The whole process can be done remotely.
Run searches and enquiries
Your solicitor runs local searches and raises questions with the seller. This stage often takes 8 to 12 weeks.
Exchange contracts
Sign and exchange contracts and pay the deposit, usually 10%. You are now legally bound to buy.
Complete
Pay the balance on the completion date and get the keys.
Pay SDLT and register
Your solicitor pays the SDLT, files the return with HMRC and registers you as owner at HM Land Registry.
united-kingdom.yearly: Yearly costs are council tax, which may include a second home premium, plus a self assessment tax return and income tax if you let the home.

united-states.name: United States
steps: Check the state rules
Confirm the state you are buying in does not restrict buyers from your country. Rules differ by state and some only cover farmland or land near military bases.
Sign up with a buyer's agent
Agents must now have a written agreement with you before showing homes. It sets out how much the agent is paid and who pays it.
Make an offer
Put your price and conditions in a written offer. You can ask the seller to pay all or part of your agent's commission.
Do the checks
Get a home inspection and a title search so you know the condition of the house and that the title is clean.
Close and record the deed
Pay the balance and closing costs at closing. The deed is then recorded with the county.
Set up your tax filing
If you rent the home out, decide between 30% tax on gross rent or the net-income election, which needs Form W-8ECI and a yearly Form 1040-NR.
united-states.yearly: Expect local property tax, which is often around 1% of value but varies widely by city, plus insurance and upkeep. If you rent it out you also file a US tax return each year when you use the net-income election.

canada.name: Canada
steps: Check if you can buy
Until January 1, 2027, non-Canadians cannot buy homes in census metropolitan areas or census agglomerations unless an exception applies. Check the location and your status first.
Check provincial foreign buyer taxes
Ontario charges foreign buyers 25% and British Columbia charges 20% in some regions. These taxes can cost more than the rest of the purchase costs combined.
Hire a real estate lawyer
The lawyer checks the title, handles the funds and registers the transfer. Ask for a written fee estimate first.
Make an offer
Sign a purchase agreement with your price and conditions, such as a home inspection.
Close the sale
On closing day you pay the balance plus land transfer tax and fees through your lawyer, and the home is registered in your name.
Arrange rental tax filings
If you rent it out, name a Canadian agent to withhold tax, consider filing Form NR6, and file a Section 216 return each year.
canada.yearly: Expect municipal property tax, from about 0.3% to 2.1% of assessed value depending on the city, plus insurance and upkeep. The federal Underused Housing Tax is proposed to end from 2025, but the change was still in Bill C-15 when last checked.

japan.name: Japan
steps: Find a home and agent
Any licensed agent can show you most listings. Many cheap homes are only advertised in Japanese, so an agent who translates helps.
Submit a written offer
Send a non-binding purchase application with your price and conditions. Non-residents usually pay cash, since Japanese banks rarely lend to them.
Hear the property explanation
Before the contract, a licensed specialist must explain the property's legal status. This can be done by video call.
Sign and pay a deposit
Sign the sale contract and pay a deposit of about 5-10%. If you pull out after this, you lose the deposit.
Pay and register

On settlement day you pay the balance and get the keys, and a judicial scrivener registers the transfer at the Legal Affairs Bureau. Since October 5, 2026 all buyers must show proof of nationality when registering.
File reports and name a tax representative
Non-residents must report the purchase to the Bank of Japan within 20 days under the Foreign Exchange Act. You also need a tax representative with a Japanese address to receive and pay tax bills.
japan.yearly: Expect fixed asset tax of 1.4% and city planning tax of up to 0.3% of assessed value, which is usually well below market value. Add the cost of a tax representative and, for apartments, monthly management and repair fund fees.

dominican-republic.name: Dominican Republic
steps: Get a tax ID (RNC)
Get your RNC at a DGII office with your passport, or through a lawyer with a notarized power of attorney. You need it to sign and to register the title.
Check the title
Have a Dominican lawyer confirm a clean title at the Title Registry, with no liens or lawsuits, and that IPI tax, utilities and condo fees are paid.
Sign a promise of sale
Sign the promise of sale contract and pay a deposit, usually 10-20%. It usually sets a 30 to 60 day window to complete.
Sign the deed before a notary
Pay the balance and sign the deed of sale. The notary legalizes the document.
Pay the transfer tax
Pay the 3% transfer tax to DGII. The title cannot be registered until it is paid.
Register the title
Your lawyer files the deed and tax receipt at the Title Registry. The new title certificate in your name usually takes 30 to 90 days.
dominican-republic.yearly: Most single homes under about $150,000 pay no IPI property tax because they fall under the threshold, but expect condo fees, utilities and upkeep. A 2026 tax law (Law 30-26) sets a 10% tax on gains when an individual sells, though its regulations were still in draft in October 2026.

mexico.name: Mexico
steps: Check the restricted zone
Foreigners cannot hold title directly within 50 km of the coast or 100 km of a border. Outside that zone you can own in your own name.
Choose how to hold title
In the restricted zone use a bank trust (fideicomiso), where a Mexican bank holds title for you, or a Mexican company. The foreign ministry (SRE) permit cost MXN 21,650 for a trust in 2026.
Check the title
Verify the seller's title, check for liens and disputes, and confirm the land is not ejido land, which cannot be sold normally.
Sign the purchase contract
Sign a contract that sets the price, payment terms and conditions. Do not wire a deposit until the documents and title have been reviewed.
Close with a notary
A public notary prepares and signs the public deed (escritura). A separate buyer's lawyer is recommended for an independent review.
Register the deed
The notary registers the deed in the Public Registry. Keep the final escritura and registration records.
mexico.yearly: Yearly costs include the local property tax (predial), usually 0.05% to 1.2% of the official cadastral value, which is often well below market value. In the restricted zone add the bank trust fee, about US$450 to US$1,000 a year, plus HOA fees, insurance and upkeep.

bulgaria.name: Bulgaria
steps: Check what you can own
Non-EU citizens can buy apartments and buildings in their own name but not land. To buy a house with its plot, a non-EU buyer usually sets up a Bulgarian company.
Hire a lawyer and check the property
A lawyer checks the title and debts, which usually takes 5 to 10 business days.
Sign a preliminary contract
Pay a deposit, usually 10%. If you pull out you lose it, and if the seller pulls out they owe you double.
Get your documents ready
You need your passport and a Bulgarian personal tax number from the National Revenue Agency. Payments of EUR 5,113 or more must go by bank transfer.
Sign the deed before a notary

Sign the notarial deed before a notary in the property's district, with a sworn translator if you do not speak Bulgarian. The notary files it with the Registry Agency, usually in 1 to 3 business days.
Declare the property to the municipality
File a tax declaration with the local municipality within 2 months of buying, and move the utility accounts into your name.
bulgaria.yearly: Yearly costs are low: municipal property tax is 0.01% to 0.45% of the tax assessment value, with a 5% discount if paid in full by April 30, plus a municipal waste collection fee. Owning through a company adds about EUR 500 to 1,500 a year in running costs.
